## 2 Many touches suffice

A key tool that is available in the study of percolation under the hypothesis that $p>p_{c}$ , but not under the mere hypothesis that $\mathrm{P}_{p}(o\leftrightarrow\infty)>0$ , is sprinkling: one can often deduce a strong statement about percolation at $p$ from a weaker statement about percolation at $p^{\prime}\in(p_{c},p)$ . In this section we will deduce Theorem 2 from the following a priori weaker proposition. The main goal of our paper is to prove this proposition. The proposition is formulated in terms of the following random variable. For a finite set of vertices $S$ , define

$$ \displaystyle\Psi(S)\coloneqq\big|\{e\in\partial S\colon e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\infty\}\big|. $$

#### Proposition 2.1.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be an infinite connected transitive graph. Let $p\in[0,1]$ be such that $\mathrm{P}_{p}(o\leftrightarrow\infty)>0$ . For all $q\in(p,1)$ and for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ , there exists $c>0$ such that for every finite set of vertices $S$ and for every positive integer $t$ with $t\leq c\,\Phi(S)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{q}(\Psi(S)\geq t)\geq(1-\varepsilon)^{t}. $$

The proof that Proposition 2.1 implies Theorem 2 relies on a variant of a well-known sprinkling argument: if two $p$ clusters touch at many places, then the probability that they do not merge at $p+\varepsilon$ is small. Here we use a variant of this statement, which asserts that a $p$ -cluster has low probability to touch a $(p+\varepsilon)$ -cluster at many places without being contained in it. The proof itself is a simple elaboration of an argument from [24, Theorem 1.1, $(ii)\Rightarrow(iii)$ ].

#### Proof of Theorem 2 given Proposition 2.1.

Let $p>p_{c}$ . Choose $q\in(p_{c},p)$ and let $\varepsilon>0$ be such that $(1-q)(1-\varepsilon)=(1-p)$ . By Proposition 2.1 applied with the same parameter $q$ but with $\varepsilon/2$ and some $p^{\prime}\in(p_{c},q)$ in place of “ $\varepsilon$ ” and “ $p$ ”, there exists $h>0$ such that for every finite set of vertices $C$ and for every positive integer $t$ with $t\leq h\,\Phi(C)$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{q}(\Psi(C)\geq t)\geq\big(1-\varepsilon/2\big)^{t}. $$

Now let $S$ be a finite set of vertices and let $n\geq 1/h$ . We will show that the displayed equation in Theorem 2 holds with $c:=h\varepsilon/4>0$ . This is sufficient to conclude our proof because if needed, one may reduce the constant $c$ to ensure that the statement also holds for $n\leq 1/h$ . Define $t:=\lfloor hn\rfloor$ , and note that $t$ is a positive integer satisfying $hn/2\leq t\leq hn$ . Let $\omega$ and $\zeta$ be independent percolation configurations with $\omega\sim\mathrm{P}_{q}$ and $\zeta\sim\mathrm{P}_{\varepsilon}$ . Note that $\omega\cup\zeta\sim\mathrm{P}_{p}$ thanks to our choice of $\varepsilon$ . Consider the event

$$ \mathcal{E}\coloneqq\{S\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\zeta}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\zeta}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\zeta}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\zeta}}}}\infty\}\cap\big\{\big|\{e\in\partial\mathcal{C}_{S}(\omega\cup\zeta):e\xleftrightarrow{\omega}\infty\}\big|\geq t\big\}. $$

On the one hand, by conditioning on $\mathcal{C}_{S}(\omega\cup\zeta)$ and applying independence,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) \displaystyle=\sum_{C}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{C}_{S}=C)\cdot\mathrm{P}_{q}(\Psi(C)\geq t), $$

where the sum is over every finite set of vertices $C$ . If such a set $C$ satisfies $\Phi(C)\geq n$ , then by our choice of $h$ , we know that $C$ also satisfies (13). So by restricting the sum in (15),

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{C\colon\Phi(C)\geq n}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{C}_{S}=C)\cdot\big(1-\varepsilon/2\big)^{t} \displaystyle=\mathrm{P}_{p}(S\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}\infty\text{ and }\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{S})\geq n)\cdot\big(1-\varepsilon/2\big)^{t}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\leq\left(1-\varepsilon\right)^{t}. $$

Indeed, this is essentially [24, Proposition 2.1], but let us anyway sketch a proof for completeness. Define

$$ \mathcal{K}:=\left\{v\in V:v\xleftrightarrow{\omega}\infty\right\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{M}\coloneqq\mathcal{C}_{S\backslash\mathcal{K}}\left((\omega\cup\zeta)\setminus\overline{\mathcal{K}}\right). $$

Observe that

$$ \mathcal{E}=\{\mathcal{K}\cap S=\varnothing\}\cap\{|\partial\mathcal{K}\cap\partial\mathcal{M}|\geq t\}\cap\{\zeta\cap\partial\mathcal{K}\cap\partial\mathcal{M}=\varnothing\}. $$

Now a.s. if $\mathcal{K}\cap S=\varnothing$ and $|\partial\mathcal{K}\cap\partial\mathcal{M}|\geq t$ , then by independence,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}\mid\mathcal{K},\mathcal{M}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(\zeta\cap\partial\mathcal{K}\cap\partial\mathcal{M}=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{K},\mathcal{M})=\left(1-\varepsilon\right)^{|\partial\mathcal{K}\cap\partial\mathcal{M}|}\leq\left(1-\varepsilon\right)^{t}, $$

which immediately yields (18) upon taking expectations.

Now by (17), (18), and the fact that $t\geq hn/2$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(S\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}\infty\text{ but }\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{S})\geq n)\leq\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon/2}\right)^{t}\leq e^{-\frac{\varepsilon t}{2}}\leq e^{-\frac{\varepsilon hn}{4}}=e^{-cn}. $$

## 3 Sketch of proof

In this section, let us present a sketch of the proof of Proposition 2.1. Fix a connected finite set $S$ in the graph $G$ and consider percolation restricted to the complement of $S$ . Call an edge $e\in\partial S$ a ‘touch’ if it is connected to infinity (in this restricted configuration). Our proof relies on an exploration algorithm that witnesses these touches one after another. An important feature of our algorithm is that the set of revealed edges of our $p$ -percolation remains connected throughout the process. We will first describe a toy version of this algorithm and then explain how to modify it for the final construction.

#### Toy algorithm.

Pick a vertex that is midway between $S$ and infinity, and explore its cluster $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ . Here midway means that the vertex has constant probability to connect to both $S$ and $\infty$ . Then pick a vertex that is midway between $S$ and $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ , and explore its cluster $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ . Note that at this stage, $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ can at best reach the external vertex boundary of $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ because the boundary of $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ has been revealed to be closed. Consider all edges where $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ touch, and sprinkle here to glue these two clusters together with constant probability. Continue in this manner $t$ times, obtaining sets $\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}$ , at each step choosing a point that is midway between $S$ and the previously explored sets. This construction guarantees that each exploration has at least constant probability $\alpha>0$ to connect to the previous explorations and witness a new touch. It follows that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{q}(\Psi(S)\geq t)\geq\alpha^{t}. $$

#### Improved algorithm.

To improve the probability of creating a new touch from $\alpha$ to $1-\varepsilon$ , we split each iteration into two: First, by revealing one large ball at a time, we search for a seed (a fully open ball) that is midway between $S$ and the previous explorations. Then we explore the cluster of this seed. To ensure that the search for seeds does not interact with future cluster explorations, we look for seeds in a seed layer, which is simply a low-density percolation that is independent of the original $p$ -percolation.

#### Where does $\Phi$ come into play?

Let us conclude this sketch with an important observation. In the toy algorithm, the set of all revealed edges is always connected. In contrast, in the improved algorithm, the search for seeds generates many bad balls in the seed layer that are disconnected from each other yet contain negative information. Consequently, while the toy algorithm can always be run until it witnesses all possible touches (i.e.​ all edges in the exposed boundary of $S$ ), the improved algorithm may halt after finding only order $\Phi(S)$ touches if the union of the bad balls forms a cutset from $S$ to infinity.

## 4 Finding mid-points and mid-balls

A standard observation in percolation theory is that for any sets of vertices $L$ and $R$ in a connected graph $G$ , if every vertex is connected to $L\cup R$ with constant probability, then there exists a mid-point vertex that has both constant probability to connect to $L$ and to $R$ . (See [16] for a recent example.)

Now suppose that our graph contains not just one but many disjoint paths from $L$ to $R$ . Then we can find not just one but many mid-points. In particular, even if we are given a not-too-large set of vertices $A$ that we seek to avoid, there will be at least one mid-point that is disjoint from $A$ . In this section, we present a high probability version of the above argument where we construct mid-balls instead of mid-points. We begin with the construction of one mid-ball that avoids a forbidden region $A$ .

#### Lemma 4.1.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph, and let $L$ and $R$ be disjoint sets of vertices. Let $r\geq 1$ and let $A$ be a set of vertices such that $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A)$ is not a vertex cutset from $L$ to $R$ . Let $p,\delta\in[0,1]$ be such that for all $v\in V$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v)\leftrightarrow L\cup R)\geq 1-\delta. $$

Then there exists a ball $B$ of radius $r$ that is disjoint from $A$ and satisfies

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(B\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash R}L),\ \mathrm{P}_{p}(B\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash L}R)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A)$ does not form a vertex cutset from $L$ to $R$ , there exists a path $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}$ from $L$ to $R$ that does not visit $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A)$ . Note that $\mathrm{B}_{r}(v_{i})$ is disjoint from $A$ for all $i$ . By the FKG inequality ( $\sqrt{\mathsf{trick}}$ ) and (24), for all $i$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i})\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash R}L)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}\quad\text{or}\quad\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i})\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash L}R)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}. $$

Note that $v_{1}$ satisfies the first option and $v_{k}$ satisfies the second. So we can find some $i\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}$ such that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i})\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash R}L),\ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i+1})\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash L}R)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}. $$

Since $\mathrm{B}_{r}(v_{i})$ contains $\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i})$ and $\mathrm{B}_{r-1}(v_{i+1})$ , the ball $B:=\mathrm{B}_{r}(v_{i})$ satisfies (25). ∎

By adding a stronger cutset condition and repeatedly applying the above lemma, we next construct many disjoint mid-balls between two sets.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph, and let $L$ and $R$ be disjoint sets of vertices. Let $r,\ell\geq 1$ and let $A$ be a finite set of vertices such that every vertex cutset from $L$ to $R$ has size at least

$$ \sup_{v\in V}|\mathrm{B}_{2r}(v)|\cdot\big(|A|+\ell\big). $$

Let $p,\delta\in[0,1]$ be such that (24) is satisfied. Then there exist balls $B_{1},\dots,B_{\ell}$ of radius $r$ that are disjoint from each other and from $A$ such that for all $i$

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(B_{i}\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash R}L),\ \mathrm{P}_{p}(B_{i}\xleftrightarrow{V\backslash L}R)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}. $$

#### Proof.

By induction, it suffices to show that for all $i\in\{1,\dots,\ell\}$ , given any balls $B_{1},\dots,B_{i-1}$ of radius $r$ , there exists a ball $B_{i}$ of radius $r$ that satisfies (25) and is disjoint from

$$ A_{i}:=A\cup B_{1}\cup\cdots\cup B_{i-1}. $$

Lemma 4.1 guarantees that such a ball $B_{i}$ exists if we are able to verify that $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A_{i})$ is not a vertex cutset from $L$ to $R$ . Let $u_{j}$ be the centre of the ball $B_{j}$ for each $j\leq i-1$ , and let $U:=A\cup\{u_{1},\dots,u_{i-1}\}$ . Since $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A_{i})\subset\mathrm{B}_{2r}(U)$ and $|U|<|A|+\ell$ ,

$$ |\mathrm{B}_{r}(A_{i})|\leq\max_{v\in U}|\mathrm{B}_{2r}(v)|\cdot|U|<\sup_{v\in V}|\mathrm{B}_{2r}(v)|\left(|A|+\ell\right). $$

So by (28), $\mathrm{B}_{r}(A_{i})$ is indeed not a vertex cutset from $L$ to $R$ . ∎

When we apply Lemma 4.2 in the proof of Proposition 2.1, edges on the boundary of the set called $R$ will have already been revealed to be closed. Nevertheless, we will want to connect a mid-ball given by Lemma 4.2 to $R$ with high probability. To salvage the situation, we will sprinkle by a small amount $\eta>0$ on the boundary of $R$ and apply the following standard observation about the (non-)effect of thinning on connection probabilities.

#### Lemma 4.3.

For all $p,\eta\in(0,1)$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists $\alpha>0$ such that the following holds. Let $B$ and $R$ be sets of vertices in a graph $H=(V,E)$ . Consider independent configurations

$$ \omega\sim\mathrm{P}_{p}^{V\setminus R}\quad\text{and}\quad\xi\sim\mathrm{P}_{\eta}^{\partial R}. $$

If $\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\leftrightarrow R)\geq 1-\alpha$ , then

$$ \mathbb{P}(B\xleftrightarrow{\,\omega\cup\xi\,}R)\geq 1-\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

The conclusion is trivial if $B$ intersects $R$ , so let us assume that $B$ does not intersect $R$ . Let $T$ be the (random) number of edges $e\in\partial R$ such that $e\xleftrightarrow{\omega}B$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}R)=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-p)^{T}\right]\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{P}(B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}R)=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\eta)^{T}\right]. $$

In particular, for any constant $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}R)\geq(1-p)^{t}\cdot\mathbb{P}(T\leq t), $$

and hence for any $\alpha>0$ satisfying $\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}R)\leq\alpha$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(B\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 9.25494pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 6.2437pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\xleftrightarrow{\omega\cup\xi}}}}R\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\eta)^{T}\mathrm{1}_{T\leq t}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\eta)^{T}\mathrm{1}_{T>t}\right] \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}(T\leq t)+(1-\eta)^{t}\leq\frac{\alpha}{(1-p)^{t}}+(1-\eta)^{t}. $$

It now suffices to first pick $t$ large enough to ensure that $(1-\eta)^{t}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ , then pick $\alpha>0$ small enough to ensure that $\frac{\alpha}{(1-p)^{t}}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ . ∎

## 5 Proof of Proposition 2.1

Let $q\in(p,1)$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ . Our goal is to find a constant $c>0$ such that for every finite set of vertices $S$ and for every positive integer $t$ with $t\leq c\,\Phi(S)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{q}(\big|\{e\in\partial S\colon e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\infty\}\big|\geq t)=\mathrm{P}_{q}\big(\sum_{e\in\partial S}\mathrm{1}\{e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\infty\}\geq t\big)\geq(1-\varepsilon)^{t}. $$

The proof is organised as follows: In Section 5.1, we will define various constants and ultimately the desired constant $c>0$ . These constants depend only on $G$ , $p$ , $q$ , and $\varepsilon$ . In Section 5.2, we will reduce our goal to a finite volume version. The core content of the proof is then presented in Sections 5.3–5.6.

### 5.1 Definition of the constant $c$

Pick $\eta\in(0,1)$ such that

$$ \displaystyle(1-p)(1-\eta)^{2}=1-q, $$

so that the union of $p$ -percolation and two copies of $\eta$ -percolation has the law of $q$ -percolation. Let

$$ \delta\coloneqq\min(\alpha,\varepsilon/4)^{2}, $$

where $\alpha$ is the constant guaranteed by Lemma 4.3 applied with $p$ , $\eta$ , and $\varepsilon/4$ in place of “ $\varepsilon$ ”. Pick $r\geq 1$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{r-1}\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq 1-\delta, $$

which exists because $\mathrm{P}_{p}(o\leftrightarrow\infty)>0$ and hence $\lim_{R\to\infty}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{R}\leftrightarrow\infty)=1$ . Define

$$ b:=\max\left(|\mathrm{B}_{r}^{\circ}|,|\mathrm{B}_{r}|\right), $$

and choose $\ell\geq 1$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\big(1-\eta^{b}\big)^{\ell}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. $$

In particular, this ensures that if we do $\eta$ -percolation on $\ell$ -many disjoint balls of radius $r$ , then with probability at least $1-\varepsilon/2$ , we can find a ball that is entirely open. Let $d$ be the vertex degree of $G$ , and note that $d\geq 2$ . We will show that we can take

$$ \displaystyle c\coloneqq\frac{1}{4b^{3}d\ell}. $$

### 5.2 Reduction to finite volume

Let $S$ be a finite set of vertices, and let $t$ be a positive integer such that $t\leq c\,\Phi(S)$ (which we may assume exists; otherwise the conclusion holds vacuously). Let us start by reducing (38) to a statement about percolation in a large ball. A.s., for each edge $e\in\partial S$ , the indicator of the event $\big\{e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\partial\mathrm{B}_{R+1}\big\}$ is decreasing in $R$ when $\mathrm{B}_{R}\supset S$ , and converges to the indicator of the event $\big\{e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\infty\big\}$ as $R\to\infty$ . So it suffices to show that for all $R$ such that $\mathrm{B}_{R}\supset S$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{q}\big(\sum_{e\in\partial S}\mathrm{1}\{e\xleftrightarrow{V\setminus S}\partial\mathrm{B}_{R+1}\}\geq t\big)\geq(1-\varepsilon)^{t}. $$

For the rest of the proof, fix $R$ such that $\mathrm{B}_{R}\supset S$ , and set $\Lambda\coloneqq\mathrm{B}_{R+1}$ . Let $\omega$ , $\xi,$ and $\zeta$ be independent (random) configurations such that

$$ \omega\sim\mathrm{P}_{p}^{\Lambda\setminus S}\quad\text{ and }\quad\xi,\zeta\sim\mathrm{P}_{\eta}^{\Lambda\setminus S}. $$

Note that by (39), $\omega\cup\xi\cup\zeta\sim\mathrm{P}_{q}^{\Lambda\setminus S}$ . So it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big(|\partial\mathcal{C}_{\partial\Lambda}\cap\partial S|\geq t\big)\geq(1-\varepsilon)^{t}, $$

where $\mathcal{C}_{\partial\Lambda}$ is the set of all vertices in $\Lambda\backslash S$ that are connected to $\partial\Lambda$ in $\omega\cup\xi\cup\zeta$ .

### 5.3 It suffices to create touches one by one

In this section, we deduce (47) from the following lemma, which isolates the relevant properties of a sequence of clusters that we will construct by the successive explorations described in Section 3. We will prove the lemma itself in the subsequent subsections.

#### Lemma 5.1.

There exists a sequence of (random) sets of vertices $\mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}\subset\mathcal{C}_{\partial\Lambda}$ such that the following holds. For each $i\in\{0,\ldots,t\}$ , define

$$ N_{i}:=|\partial(\mathcal{C}_{0}\cup\dots\cup\mathcal{C}_{i})\cap\partial S|. $$

Then for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{P}(N_{i-1}<N_{i}\mid N_{0}<\cdots<N_{i-1}<t)\geq 1-\varepsilon, $$

or the event being conditioned on has probability zero.

#### Completing the proof of Proposition 2.1 given Lemma 5.1.

Let $\mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}$ be the sequence given by Lemma 5.1, and for all $i$ let $N_{i}$ be as in (48). For each $i\in\{0,\ldots,t\}$ , consider the event

$$ \mathcal{E}_{i}:=\{N_{0}<\cdots<N_{i}\}\cup\{N_{i-1}\geq t\}, $$

where we set $N_{-1}:=0$ . Let $i\geq 1$ . By (49),

$$ \mathbb{P}(N_{0}<\dots<N_{i}\text{ and }N_{i-1}<t)\geq(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathbb{P}(N_{0}<\dots<N_{i-1}<t). $$

Since $N_{i-2}\leq N_{i-1}$ , we have the inclusion

$$ \mathcal{E}_{i-1}\subset\{N_{0}<\cdots<N_{i-1}<t\}\cup\{N_{i-1}\geq t\}. $$

Therefore, by applying the definition of $\mathcal{E}_{i}$ and by (51) and (52),

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(N_{0}<\dots<N_{i}\text{ and }N_{i-1}<t)+\mathbb{P}(N_{i-1}\geq t) \displaystyle\geq(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\big(\mathbb{P}(N_{0}<\dots<N_{i-1}<t)+\mathbb{P}(N_{i-1}\geq t)\big) \displaystyle\geq(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{i-1}). $$

In particular, noting that $\mathcal{E}_{t}\subset\{N_{t}\geq t\}$ and $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{0})=1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|\partial C_{\partial\Lambda}\cap\partial S|\geq t)\geq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{t})\geq(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{t-1})\geq\cdots\geq(1-\varepsilon)^{t}. $$

This establishes (47) and thus concludes the proof of the proposition. ∎

### 5.4 Choosing potential seeds

In this subsection, we apply Lemma 4.2 to construct a function $\mathsf{Seeds}$ that we will use to produce a collection of mid-balls between what has already been explored and the fixed set $S$ . We emphasise that the function $\mathsf{Seeds}$ appearing in this lemma is purely deterministic. Let us fix a choice of such a function for all subsequent subsections. Given a set of vertices $A$ , let $\mathcal{P}(A)$ denote the set of all subsets of $A$ .

#### Lemma 5.2.

There exists a function

$$ \mathsf{Seeds}:\mathcal{P}(\Lambda\backslash S)^{2}\to\mathcal{P}(\Lambda\backslash S)^{\ell} $$

with the following property. For every input $(D,K)$ satisfying

$$ K\supset\partial^{-}\!\Lambda,\quad|\partial K\cap\partial S|<t,\quad\text{and}\quad|D|\leq b\ell t, $$

the output is a sequence of sets $B_{1},\dots,B_{\ell}$ that are disjoint from each other and from $D$ such that for all $i$ , the set $B_{i}$ is a ball of radius $r$ with respect to the graph $G[\Lambda\backslash S]$ and satisfies

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}\bigl(B_{i}\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda\setminus(K\cup S)}\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K\bigr),\,\mathrm{P}_{p}\bigl(B_{i}\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda\setminus S}K\bigr)\geq 1-\sqrt{\delta}. $$

#### Proof.

Suppose that we are given sets $D,K\subset\Lambda\backslash S$ satisfying (58). We would like to define $\mathsf{Seeds}(D,K)$ to be the sequence of balls given by applying Lemma 4.2 to the graph $G[\Lambda\backslash S]$ , using the same $p$ , $\delta$ , $r$ , $\ell$ , but with $D$ in place of “ $A$ ”, and using

$$ L:=\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K\quad\text{and}\quad R:=K, $$

since (59) is immediately implied by (29) with this setup. (There may be multiple sequences satisfying the conclusion of Lemma 4.2; to define $\mathsf{Seeds}(D,K)$ , we choose a particular sequence from among all options according to an arbitrary deterministic rule.) To apply this lemma, we need to a) verify (24) and b) show that every vertex cutset in $G[\Lambda\backslash S]$ from $L$ to $R$ has size at least (28).

a) Let $v\in\Lambda\setminus S$ . Consider $B\coloneqq\mathrm{B}_{r-1}^{G[\Lambda\setminus S]}(v)$ and $B^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathrm{B}_{r-1}^{G}(v)$ , and note that either $B=B^{\prime}$ or $B^{\prime}$ is not entirely contained in $\Lambda\setminus S$ . If $B=B^{\prime}$ , then by our choice of $r$ in (41),

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda\setminus S}L\cup R) \displaystyle\geq\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda\setminus S}\partial^{+}\!S\cup\partial^{-}\!\Lambda) \displaystyle\geq\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\leftrightarrow\infty)=\mathrm{P}_{p}(B^{\prime}\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq 1-\delta. $$

If $B^{\prime}$ is not entirely contained in $\Lambda\setminus S$ , then $B$ must intersect $\partial^{+}\!S\cup\partial^{-}\!\Lambda\subset L\cup R$ , and hence $\mathrm{P}_{p}(B\xleftrightarrow{\Lambda\setminus S}L\cup R)=1.$

b) Observe that every ball of radius $2r$ in $G[\Lambda\setminus S]$ is contained in a ball of radius $2r$ in $G$ and hence has size at most $|\mathrm{B}_{2r}|\leq b^{2}$ . Conversely, any vertex cutset $W$ in $G[\Lambda\setminus S]$ from $L$ to $R$ induces an edge cutset $\overline{W}\cup(\partial K\cap\partial S)$ in $G$ that from $S$ to infinity and hence satisfies

$$ d\cdot|W|+|\partial K\cap\partial S|\geq|\overline{W}|+|\partial K\cap\partial S|\geq\Phi(S). $$

So it suffices to show that

$$ d\cdot b^{2}(|D|+\ell)+|\partial K\cap\partial S|<\Phi(S). $$

By (58), since $t\leq c\,\Phi(S)$ and by our choice of $c$ in (44),

$$ \displaystyle d\cdot b^{2}|D|+|\partial K\cap\partial S|<db^{3}\ell t+t\leq 2db^{3}\ell t\leq 2db^{3}\ell\cdot c\,\Phi(S)=\frac{1}{2}\Phi(S). $$

Furthermore, since $t$ is a positive integer satisfying $t\leq c\,\Phi(S)$ , we have that $\Phi(S)\geq 1/c$ , and hence by our choice of $c$ in (44)

$$ d\cdot b^{2}\ell\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{c}\leq\frac{1}{2}\Phi(S). $$

By combining (65) with (66), we obtain (64) as required. ∎

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $D,K\subset\Lambda\setminus S$ be sets satisfying (58), and let $B\in\mathsf{Seeds}(D,K)$ . Then

### 5.5 Growing seeds

In this section, given a ball outputted by the $\mathsf{Seeds}$ function from the previous subsection, we will describe how to construct a certain cluster of the ball via a two-step exploration.

#### Definition 5.4.

Given sets $D,K\subset\Lambda\setminus S$ satisfying (58), and given $B\in\mathsf{Seeds}(D,K)$ , define

$$ \mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)\coloneqq\mathcal{C}_{1}\cup\mathcal{C}_{2}, $$

where

$$ \mathcal{C}_{1}:=\mathcal{C}_{B}(\omega\setminus\overline{K})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{C}_{2}:=V\left(\partial\left(\mathcal{C}_{1}\setminus K\right)\cap\partial K\cap\xi\right), $$

i.e.​ $\mathcal{C}_{2}$ is the set of all vertices contained in a $\xi$ -open edge $uv$ with $u\in\mathcal{C}_{1}\backslash K$ and $v\in K$ .

Here are three elementary properties of $\mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)$ that are evident from its construction.

#### Remark 5.5.

Almost surely, $\mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)$ is connected in $\omega\cup\xi\cup B^{\circ}.$

#### Remark 5.6.

Almost surely, $\mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)\text{ intersects }\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K$ if and only if

$$ B\xleftrightarrow{\omega\backslash\overline{K}}\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K, $$

and $\mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)\text{ intersects $K$}$ if and only if

$$ B\xleftrightarrow{(\omega\setminus\overline{K})\cup(\xi\cap\partial K)}K. $$

#### Remark 5.7.

For every fixed set $C\subset\Lambda\setminus S$ , the event $\{\mathcal{C}_{D,K}(B)=C\}$ is measurable with respect to

$$ \omega\cap\overline{C}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\xi\cap\partial(C\setminus K)\cap\partial K. $$

### 5.6 Proof of Lemma 5.1

Building upon the previous subsections, we can now construct our sequence of random sets.

Construction of $\mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}$ Let us recursively define a sequence of sets $\mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}\subset\Lambda\backslash S$ and a sequence $\mathcal{S}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{t}$ such that for all $j$ , $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ is a collection of subsets of $\Lambda\setminus S$ satisfying

$$ \sum_{B\in\mathcal{S}_{j}}|B|\leq b\ell. $$

Start with

$$ \mathcal{S}_{0}=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{C}_{0}=\partial^{-}\!\Lambda. $$

Now let $i\in\{1,\dots,t\}$ , and suppose that we have defined $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{j}$ for all $j<i$ , but we have not yet defined $\mathcal{S}_{i}$ or $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ . Consider

$$ \mathcal{D}:=\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{S}_{j}}B\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{K}:=\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}\mathcal{C}_{j}. $$

If $|\partial S\cap\partial\mathcal{K}|\geq t$ , then set

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}:=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{C}_{j}:=\varnothing\quad\text{for all $j\geq i$.} $$

Now instead suppose that $|\partial S\cap\partial\mathcal{K}|<t$ . By applying (75) to all $j<i$ , we have that

$$ |\mathcal{D}|\leq b\ell i\leq b\ell t. $$

Thus, $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ satisfy (58). So $\mathsf{Seeds}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K})$ is a sequence balls in $G[\Lambda\backslash S]$ with the properties guaranteed by Lemma 5.2, and the cluster $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K}}(B)$ from Section 5.5 is well-defined for any $B\in\mathsf{Seeds}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K})$ . Define

$$ \mathcal{S}_{i}:=\mathsf{Seeds}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K}), $$

and note that this choice satisfies (75) with $j=i$ . Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the first ball in the (ordered) sequence of balls given by $\mathsf{Seeds}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K})$ such that $\zeta(e)=1$ for all $e\in\mathcal{B}^{\circ}$ ; if no such ball exists, then set $\mathcal{B}:=\varnothing$ . If $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K}}(\mathcal{B})$ intersects $\partial^{+}\!S\setminus\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ , then set

$$ C_{i}:=\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{K}}(\mathcal{B}); $$

otherwise, set

$$ \mathcal{C}_{j}:=\varnothing\quad\text{for all $j\geq i$}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\mathcal{S}_{j}:=\varnothing\quad\text{for all $j\geq i+1$}. $$

Properties of $\mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}$ Note that for all $i$ , if $\mathcal{C}_{i}=\varnothing$ then $\mathcal{C}_{j}=\varnothing$ for all $j>i$ . Moreover, for all $i\in\{1,\dots,t\}$ , if $\mathcal{C}_{j}\not=\varnothing$ for all $j\leq i$ , then by Remark 5.5 and our choice of $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ , we have $\mathcal{C}_{i}\subset\mathcal{C}_{\partial\Lambda}$ . Therefore,

$$ \mathcal{C}_{0},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}\subset\mathcal{C}_{\partial\Lambda}. $$

Let $i\in\{1,\dots,t\}$ . By construction of $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ , we have that if $\mathcal{C}_{i}\not=\varnothing$ then $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ intersects $\partial^{+}\!S\backslash\bigcup_{j<i}\mathcal{C}_{j}$ . In particular,

$$ N_{i}>N_{i-1}\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\mathcal{C}_{i}\neq\varnothing, $$

where $N_{i}$ is as given in (48). So in order to establish (49), it suffices to show

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i}\neq\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}\not=\varnothing\text{ for all }j\leq i-1\text{ and }N_{i-1}<t)\geq 1-\varepsilon, $$

whenever the event being conditioned on has non-zero probability. To this end, fix non-empty sets of vertices $C_{0},\dots,C_{i-1}$ such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1)>0$ , and such that $|\partial K\cap\partial S|<t$ where $K:=\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}C_{j}$ . (If no such sets exist, then there is nothing to prove.) By averaging over all choices for these sets, to establish (84), it suffices to show that

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i}\not=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1)\geq 1-\varepsilon. $$

Notice that there exists a unique sequence of deterministic collections $S_{0},\dots,S_{i}$ such that if $\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}$ for all $j\leq i-1$ , then $\mathcal{S}_{j}=S_{j}$ for all $j\leq i$ . Now define

$$ D\coloneqq\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}\bigcup_{B\in S_{j}}B\quad\text{and}\quad K\coloneqq\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}C_{j}. $$

Note that by repeatedly applying Remark 5.7, the event that $\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}$ for all $j\leq i-1$ is measurable with respect to

$$ \zeta\cap D^{\circ},\quad\omega\cap\overline{K},\quad\xi\cap K^{\circ}. $$

Note that these three configurations are independent of

$$ \zeta\cap\bigcup_{B\in S_{i}}S_{i}^{\circ} $$

because $\mathsf{Seeds}(D,K)$ only outputs balls that are disjoint from $D$ . So, as in the construction of $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ , letting $\mathcal{B}$ be the first $\zeta$ -open ball in $\mathcal{S}_{i}$ ( $\mathcal{B}=\varnothing$ if none exists), by our choice of $\ell$ in (43),

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1)=\prod_{B\in S_{i}}(1-\eta^{|B^{\circ}|})\leq(1-\eta^{b})^{\ell}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. $$

Now consider a fixed $B\in\mathcal{S}_{i}$ . By Remark 5.6

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i}\not=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1\text{ and }\mathcal{B}=B) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K\xleftrightarrow{\omega\setminus\overline{K}}B\xleftrightarrow{(\omega\setminus\overline{K})\cup(\xi\cap\partial K)}K\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1\text{ and }\mathcal{B}=B). $$

Note that the event that

$$ \partial^{+}\!S\setminus K\xleftrightarrow{\omega\setminus\overline{K}}B\xleftrightarrow{(\omega\setminus\overline{K})\cup(\xi\cap\partial K)}K $$

is measurable with respect to

$$ \omega\setminus\overline{K}\quad\text{and}\quad\xi\cap\partial K, $$

whereas the event that $\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}$ for all $j\leq i-1$ and $\mathcal{B}=B$ is measurable with respect to the configurations in (87) and (88). So these two events are independent. Hence,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i}\not=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1\text{ and }\mathcal{B}=B)=\mathbb{P}(\partial^{+}\!S\setminus K\xleftrightarrow{\omega\setminus\overline{K}}B\xleftrightarrow{(\omega\setminus\overline{K})\cup(\xi\cap\partial K)}K). $$

So by Lemma 5.3 and averaging over all choices of $B$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i}\not=\varnothing\mid\mathcal{C}_{j}=C_{j}\text{ for all }j\leq i-1\text{ and }\mathcal{B}\not=\varnothing)\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. $$

By combining equations (89), (95), and using that $(1-\varepsilon/2)^{2}\geq 1-\varepsilon$ , we establish (85), as desired. ∎

## 6 Deducing Theorem 1

In this section, we deduce Theorem 1 from Theorem 2. The first inequality appearing in Theorem 1, concerning the volume of $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ , is essentially an immediate corollary of Theorem 2. On the other hand, to deduce the second inequality from Theorem 2, concerning the radius of $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ , we will require the following geometric proposition.

#### Proposition 6.1.

Let $G$ be an infinite bounded-degree graph. Suppose that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\Phi(n)\geq\varepsilon n^{1/2}$ for all $n\geq 1$ . Then there exists $\delta>0$ such that for every finite, connected set of vertices $A$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\partial A|\geq\delta\cdot\operatorname{diam}(A). $$

This proposition is sharp in the sense that the hypothesis $\Phi(n)\geq\varepsilon n^{1/2}$ cannot be weakened. Indeed, consider the graph induced by $\{(x,y)\colon|y|\leq f(x)\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ for functions $f$ that are only slightly sublinear. Before proving the proposition, let us conclude our proof of Theorem 1.

#### Proof Theorem 1 given Proposition 6.1.

The first displayed inequality in Theorem 1 follows from Theorem 2 applied with $S=\{o\}$ , because for all $n\geq 1$ , if $n\leq|\mathcal{C}_{o}|<\infty$ then $\Phi(\mathcal{C}_{o})\geq\Phi(n)$ .

As for the second displayed inequality in Theorem 1, let us start by explaining why we may assume without loss of generality that there exists a constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\Phi(n)\geq\varepsilon n^{1/2}$ for all $n$ : by [26, Lemma 7.2] (see also [27, Chapter 6.7]) every infinite transitive graph that does not satisfy such a two-dimensional isoperimetric inequality cannot have at least two-dimensional volume growth, and hence by Gromov and Trofimov [22, 30] (see also [32, Theorem 5.11]) is quasi-isometric to $\mathbb{Z}$ , and therefore satisfies $p_{c}=1$ . Now the second displayed inequality in Theorem 1 follows from Theorem 2 because for all $n$ , if $o\leftrightarrow\partial\mathrm{B}_{n}$ but $o\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}\infty$ , then $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{C}_{o})\geq n$ , and hence by Proposition 6.1, $\Phi(C_{o})\geq\delta n$ for some constant $\delta>0$ . ∎

All that remains is to prove the geometric proposition itself.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Let $A$ be a finite, connected set of vertices, and let $m$ be its diameter. Fix some vertex $o\in A$ . Given integers $k$ and $r$ , let $A_{k,r}$ be the set of all vertices $v\in A$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(o,v)\in[k-r,k+r]$ , and let $A_{k}\coloneqq A_{k,0}$ . Define

$$ f(k,r):=|A_{k,r}|\quad\text{and}\quad g(k,r):=|\partial A_{k,r}\cap\partial A|. $$

Given $k\in[m]:=\{0,\dots,m\}$ , let $r(k)$ be the smallest non-negative integer $r$ such that

$$ g(k,r)\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}f(k,r)^{1/2}, $$

which exists because by applying our isoperimetric inequality to $A$ ,

$$ g(k,m)=|\partial A|\geq\varepsilon|A|^{1/2}=\varepsilon f(k,m)^{1/2}. $$

Without loss of generality, assume that $\varepsilon<1$ . Let us prove by induction that for all $r\in[r(k)]$ ,

$$ f(k,r)\geq\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}\right)^{2}(r+1)^{2}, $$

where $d$ is the maximum vertex degree of $G$ . When $r=0$ , (100) holds trivially because $A$ is connected and hence $f(k,0)\geq 1$ . Now let $r\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ , and suppose that (100) holds at $r-1$ . By applying our isoperimetric inequality to $A_{k,r-1}$ ,

$$ d|A_{k-r}|+d|A_{k+r}|+g(k,r-1)\geq|\partial A_{k,r-1}|\geq\varepsilon f(k,r-1)^{1/2}. $$

So by the negation of (98) and by (100) at $r-1$ ,

$$ |A_{k-r}|+|A_{k+r}|\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{2d}f(k,r-1)^{1/2}\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{2d}\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}r\geq\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}\right)^{2}(2r+1), $$

and hence,

$$ \displaystyle f(k,r) \displaystyle=f(k,r-1)+|A_{k-r}|+|A_{k+r}| \displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}\right)^{2}r^{2}+\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}\right)^{2}(2r+1)=\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{6d}\right)^{2}(r+1)^{2}, $$

completing our induction. Now by (98) and (100) at $r=r(k)$ ,

$$ g(k,r(k))\geq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{12d}(r(k)+1). $$

Note that the collection of intervals

$$ I_{k}:=\left[k-r(k)-1/2,k+r(k)+1/2\right]\quad\text{for $k\in[m]$} $$

trivially covers $[0,m]$ . Consider a minimal family of such intervals covering $[0,m]$ . Enumerate the intervals in this family, from left to right, according to each interval’s left endpoint, and observe that by minimality, the even-indexed intervals are disjoint and the odd-indexed intervals are disjoint. Hence there exists a subset $L\subset[m]$ such that the intervals $I_{k}$ for $k\in L$ are disjoint from each other and satisfy $\sum_{k\in L}|I_{k}|\geq m/2$ . (We could have alternatively used Vitali’s covering lemma.) So by (105) and the fact that each $I_{k}$ has length $|I_{k}|\leq 2(r(k)+1)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\partial A|\geq\sum_{k\in L}g(k,r(k))\geq\sum_{k\in L}\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{12d}(r(k)+1)\geq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{24d}\sum_{k\in L}|I_{k}|\geq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{48d}m. $$

## 7 Collecting mass

Let $G$ be an infinite connected transitive graph. By Theorem 2, for all $p>p_{c}$ , there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for every finite set of vertices $S$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(S\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq 1-e^{-c\,\Phi(S)}, $$

which is sharp up to the choice of $c$ . The following theorem says that with high probability, $S$ is also connected to many vertices within its neighbourhood at every scale. Formally, given non-empty finite set of vertices $S$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , define

$$ \mathcal{C}_{S}^{n}=\big\{v\in\mathrm{B}_{n}(S):v\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{n}(S)}S\big\}. $$

#### Theorem 3.

For all $p>p_{c}$ there exist $c>0$ such that for every finite non-empty set of vertices $S$ we have,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}\big(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\quad|\mathcal{C}_{S}^{n}|\geq v_{n}\big)\geq 1-\sum_{n\geq|S|}e^{-c\Phi(n)}, $$

where $v_{n}=v_{n}(S)$ for $n\geq 0$ is defined implicitly by

$$ \int_{|S|}^{v_{n}}\frac{1}{c\,\Phi(t)}\,dt=n. $$

#### Remark 7.1.

Theorem 3 may be viewed as an analogue for percolation of the well-known relationship between return probabilities and isoperimetry for random walks (see [27, Chapter 6.7]).

#### Remark 7.2.

Essentially, $v_{n}(S)$ is the lower bound on the size of the neighbourhood $\mathrm{B}_{n}(S)$ that one obtains simply by recursively applying the isoperimetric function to smaller neighbourhoods. If $G$ is of polynomial growth then $v_{n}(S)\asymp\mathrm{B}_{n}(S)$ . On the other hand, if $G$ is of exponential growth, then by a result of Coulhon and Saloff-Coste, at worst $\Phi(x)\asymp x/\log x$ , in which case $v_{n}\asymp e^{c\sqrt{n}}$ . If $G$ is non-amenable (i.e. $\Phi(x)\gtrsim x$ ), then we always have $v_{n}\gtrsim e^{cn}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $p\in(p_{c},1)$ and let $c^{\prime}>0$ be the constant guaranteed by Theorem 1 (it suffices to consider only $p<1$ ). We will show that the conclusion of our theorem holds with $c:=\min\big(\frac{-c^{\prime}}{4d\log(1-p)},\frac{1}{2d}\big)$ , where $d$ is the vertex degree of $G$ . Let $S$ be a finite set of vertices, and let $v_{n}$ be defined by (111). Consider some non-negative integer $n$ . Since $\Phi$ is increasing,

$$ v_{n+1}-v_{n}\leq\int_{v_{n}}^{v_{n+1}}\frac{\Phi(v_{n+1})}{\Phi(t)}\,dt=c\,\Phi(v_{n+1}). $$

By rearranging this inequality and using that $c\leq 1/2d$ and $\Phi(v_{n+1})\leq dv_{n+1}$ , we obtain $v_{n+1}\leq 2v_{n}$ . Since $\Phi(2x)\leq 2\Phi(x)$ for all $x$ , it follows that $\Phi(v_{n+1})\leq\Phi(2v_{n})\leq 2\Phi(v_{n})$ . Therefore,

$$ v_{n+1}-v_{n}\leq 2c\,\Phi(v_{n}). $$

For each $n\geq 0$ , let $M_{n}=|\mathcal{C}_{S}^{n}|$ . Observe that $M_{0}=|S|=v_{0}$ . By a union bound,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\forall n\;\;M_{n}\geq v_{n})\geq 1-\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathrm{P}_{p}(M_{n}\geq v_{n}\text{ but }M_{n+1}<v_{n+1}). $$

Since $M_{n}$ is always an integer, the summands here are zero whenever $[v_{n},v_{n+1})$ does not contain an integer. So let $I$ be the set of all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that the interval $[v_{n},v_{n+1})$ contains an integer, and consider a fixed $n\in I$ . Let $\mathcal{W}$ be the set of all edges $e\in\partial\mathrm{B}_{n+1}(S)$ such that $e\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{n+1}(S)}S$ . By (113), when $M_{n}\geq v_{n}$ and $M_{n+1}<v_{n+1}$ , we know that

$$ M_{n+1}-M_{n}\leq 2c\,\Phi(v_{n}), $$

and hence $|\mathcal{W}|\leq 2cd\Phi(v_{n})$ . By revealing our percolation configuration in $\mathrm{B}_{n+1}(S)$ , we can determine the set $\mathcal{W}$ without revealing the status of its edges. Moreover, if every edge in $W$ is closed then $S$ is not connected to infinity. So by independence

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}\big(M_{n}\geq v_{n}\text{ but }M_{n+1}<v_{n+1}\big)\cdot(1-p)^{2cd\Phi(v_{n})}\leq\mathrm{P}_{p}(v_{n}\leq|\mathcal{C}_{S}|<\infty). $$

So by rearranging, since $c^{\prime}$ has the properties guaranteed by Theorem 1,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}\big(M_{n}\geq v_{n}\text{ but }M_{n+1}<v_{n+1}\big)\leq\frac{e^{-c^{\prime}\Phi(v_{n})}}{(1-p)^{2cd\Phi(v_{n})}}\leq e^{-c\Phi(v_{n})}, $$

where the last inequality follows from our formula for $c$ . Finally, plugging (116) in (114) yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}_{p}(\forall n\;\;M_{n}\geq v_{n}) \displaystyle\geq 1-\sum_{n\in I}e^{-c\,\Phi(v_{n})}\geq 1-\sum_{n\geq|S|}e^{-c\,\Phi(n)}. $$

#### Remark 7.3.

The argument in this section can be seen as a version of the ‘isoperimetry from tail estimates’ argument in [29], restricted to balls.

## 8 Supercritical sharpness on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$

In this section, we will explain how to derive the following Grimmett–Marstrand slab theorem from Theorem 3. Fix $d\geq 3$ and consider percolation on the hypercubic lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ . For each $\ell\geq 1$ , consider a slab of thickness $\ell$ , given by

$$ \mathbb{S}_{\ell}:=\mathbb{Z}^{2}\times\{-\ell,\ldots,\ell\}^{d-2} $$

#### Theorem 4 (Grimmett–Marstrand, 1990).

For all $p>p_{c}(\mathbb{Z}^{d})$ , there exists $\ell\geq 1$ such that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(0\xleftrightarrow{\mathbb{S}_{\ell}}\infty)>0. $$

We will apply the following well-known lemma, which follows from a standard static renormalisation scheme. We provide its proof for the reader’s convenience. We write $\mathrm{B}_{k}(n)$ as shorthand for $\mathrm{B}_{k}(e_{n})$ where $e_{n}:=(n,0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ and we set $\mathrm{B}_{k}:=\mathrm{B}_{k}(0)$ .

#### Lemma 8.1.

Let $p\in[0,1]$ . If there exists a constant $C\geq 2$ such that

$$ \lim_{k\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{k}\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{Cn}}\mathrm{B}_{k}(n))=1, $$

then there exists $\ell\geq 1$ such that $\mathrm{P}_{p}(0\xleftrightarrow{\mathbb{S}_{\ell}}\infty)>0$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that we have a constant $C\geq 2$ satisfying (120). By [25] (or a direct Peierls argument), there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that any $3C$ -dependent percolation on the usual square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ with marginals of at least $1-3\varepsilon$ has an infinite cluster almost surely. Then there exists $k<\infty$ such that

$$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{k}\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{Cn}}\mathrm{B}_{k}(n))>1-\varepsilon. $$

By the uniqueness of the infinite cluster, there exists $n_{0}<\infty$ such that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(U)>1-\varepsilon, $$

where $U$ is the event that there exists at most one cluster in the restriction of our percolation configuration to $\mathrm{B}_{n_{0}}^{\circ}$ that intersects both $\mathrm{B}_{k}$ and $\partial^{-}\!\mathrm{B}_{n_{0}}$ . Hence by equation (121), there exists $n\geq n_{0}$ such that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{k}\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{Cn}}\mathrm{B}_{k}(n))>1-\varepsilon. $$

For each edge $uv$ of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ (using the obvious inclusion), let $\zeta(uv)$ denote the indicator of the event

$$ \{(nu+\mathrm{B}_{k})\xleftrightarrow{nu+\mathrm{B}_{Cn}}(nv+\mathrm{B}_{k})\}\cap U(nu)\cap U(nv), $$

where $U(x)$ denotes the event $U$ translated to be centred around the vector $(x,0,\dots,0)$ . Note that $\zeta$ is a $3C$ -dependent percolation with marginals at least $1-3\varepsilon$ . Moreover, a.s., if $\zeta$ contains an infinite cluster then the restriction of our original percolation configuration to $\mathbb{S}_{Cn}$ does too. So by our choice of $C$ , we have $\mathrm{P}_{p}(0\xleftrightarrow{\mathbb{S}_{Cn}}\infty)>0$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 4.

Let $p>p_{c}(\mathbb{Z}^{d})$ . Since we are working on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , we know that $\Phi(n)\gtrsim n^{\frac{d-1}{d}}$ . So by Theorem 3 and some calculus, there exists $\delta>0$ such that

$$ \lim_{k\to\infty}\inf_{n\geq 3k}\mathrm{P}_{p}(|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}_{k}}^{n}|>\delta|\mathrm{B}_{2n}|)=1. $$

Let $C\coloneqq 2\lceil 1/\delta\rceil$ . We will show that (120) holds with $2C$ , which is sufficient to conclude our proof thanks to Lemma 8.1. To this end, let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ . Pick $k\geq 1$ such that for all $n\geq 3k$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{B}_{k}}^{n}|>\delta|\mathrm{B}_{2n}|)>1-\eta, $$

where $\eta:=\varepsilon^{C^{2}}/C$ . Now let $n\geq 3k$ . For each $i\in\{0,\ldots,C-1\}$ , define

$$ \mathcal{C}_{i}:=\{x\in\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}:x\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{Cn}(ni)}\mathrm{B}_{k}(ni)\}. $$

Since $\mathrm{B}_{Cn}(ni)\subset\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}$ , by (126) applied with $Cn$ in place of $n$ and a union bound,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}\big(|\mathcal{C}_{i}|>\delta|\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}|\text{ for all $i$}\big)\geq 1-C\eta. $$

If $|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\geq\delta|\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}|$ for all $i$ , by a density argument, there exist indices $i\neq j$ such that $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ intersects $\mathcal{C}_{j}$ . Since $|ni-nj|\leq Cn$ , we have $\mathrm{B}_{Cn}(nj)\subset\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}(nj)$ and therefore $\mathrm{B}_{k}(ni)\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}(ni)}\mathrm{B}_{k}(nj)$ . Since there are only at most $C^{2}$ pairs of indices, by the $\sqrt{\mathsf{trick}}$ , we deduce that there exists fixed indices $i\not=j$ such that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{k}(ni)\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{2Cn}(ni)}\mathrm{B}_{k}(nj))>1-(C\eta)^{1/C^{2}}\geq 1-\varepsilon. $$

So by translation invariance, $m\coloneqq|i-j|n\geq n$ satisfies

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathrm{B}_{k}\xleftrightarrow{\mathrm{B}_{2Cm}}\mathrm{B}_{k}(m))\geq 1-\varepsilon. $$

Since $n$ was arbitrary, this establishes that (120) holds. ∎

#### Remark 8.2.

Theorem 4 says that for all $p>p_{c}(\mathbb{Z}^{d})$ , we have percolation in a sufficiently thick slab. In particular, we certainly have percolation in the half-space $\mathbb{H}:=\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{Z}^{d-1}$ . Let us sketch how to deduce that we have percolation in the half-space directly from Theorem 2, without going via slabs: Consider the region between $\mathrm{B}_{n}$ and $S:=\partial^{-}\!\mathrm{B}_{2n}$ for some large $n$ . By Theorem 2, with probability at least $1/2$ , some constant proportion $c>0$ of the vertices in $S$ are connected to $\mathrm{B}_{n}$ . (Otherwise, by closing $\partial B_{n}$ , we can force $\mathrm{B}_{n}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 5.0pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.98611pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.40282pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\leftrightarrow}}}\infty$ with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}\cdot(1-p)^{dc|S|}$ , contradicting Theorem 2 if $c$ is small.) By considering the point of view of a uniformly random vertex in $S$ on this event, we see that $\mathrm{P}_{p}(0\xleftrightarrow{\mathbb{H}}\infty)\geq c/2>0$ , as required.

# Counting minimal cutsets and $p_{c}<1$

**Authors:** Philip Easo, Franco Severo, Vincent Tassion

## Abstract

We prove two results concerning percolation on general graphs.

We establish the converse of the classical Peierls argument: if the critical parameter for (uniform) percolation satisfies $p_{c}<1$ , then the number of minimal cutsets of size $n$ separating a given vertex from infinity is bounded above exponentially in $n$ . This resolves a conjecture of Babson and Benjamini from 1999.

We prove that $p_{c}<1$ for every uniformly transient graph. This solves a problem raised by Duminil-Copin, Goswami, Raoufi, Severo and Yadin, and provides a new proof that $p_{c}<1$ for every transitive graph of superlinear growth.

## 1. Main results

Let $G=(V,E)$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. A set of edges $F\subset E$ is called a cutset from a vertex $v$ to $\infty$ if $v$ belongs to a finite connected component of $(V,E\setminus F)$ . A cutset is called minimal if no proper subset of it is a cutset. Let $\mathcal{Q}_{n}(v)$ be the set of minimal cutsets from $v$ to $\infty$ of cardinality $n$ and consider the quantity

$$ q_{n}:=\sup_{v\in V}|\mathcal{Q}_{n}(v)|. $$

Here $\left\lvert\emptyset\right\rvert:=0$ . We emphasize that $q_{n}=\infty$ is possible, for example for $G=\mathbb{Z}$ and $n=2$ . In this paper, we are interested in cases where the number of cutsets $q_{n}$ grows at most exponentially with $n$ , and we define

$$ \kappa(G):=\sup_{n\geq 1}q_{n}^{1/n}. $$

Let $\mathrm{P}_{p}$ denote (Bernoulli bond) percolation of parameter $p\in[0,1]$ on $G$ , where each edge is open with probability $p$ independently of the other edges. Consider the percolation probabilities $\theta_{v}(p):=\mathrm{P}_{p}(v\leftrightarrow\infty)$ , where $v\leftrightarrow\infty$ denotes the event that $v$ belongs to an infinite open connected component. We define the critical parameter for uniform percolation as

$$ p_{c}^{*}(G):=\inf\{p\in[0,1]:\theta^{*}(p)>0\}, $$

where $\theta^{*}(p):=\inf_{v\in V}\theta_{v}(p)$ .

By the classical Peierls argument [Pei36] if $\kappa(G)<\infty$ , then percolation on $G$ has a uniformly percolating phase in the sense that $p_{c}^{*}(G)<1$ . Our first theorem establishes the converse.

#### Theorem 1.

For every infinite, connected, locally finite graph $G$ we have

$$ p_{c}^{*}(G)<1\iff\kappa(G)<\infty. $$

Currently, the geometric condition $\kappa(G)<\infty$ is not well understood. Our second result gives a sufficient condition based on the simple random walk. Given a vertex $v$ , let $\mathbb{P}_{v}$ be the law of a simple random walk $(X_{t})_{t=0}^{\infty}$ on $G$ starting at $v$ . We say that $G$ is uniformly transient if

$$ \inf_{v\in V}\left[d_{v}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{v}(\forall t\geq 1:\ X_{t}\neq v)\right]>0, $$

where $d_{v}$ denotes the degree of $v$ .

#### Theorem 2.

Let $G$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. If $G$ is uniformly transient, then $\kappa(G)<\infty$ .

## 2. Consequences and comments

In this section, all graphs are assumed to be infinite, connected, and locally finite. Given a set of vertices $S$ in a graph $G=(V,E)$ , we define the boundary $\partial S$ to be the set of all edges $\{u,v\}\in E$ such that $u\in S$ but $v\not\in S$ , and we define the weight $\left\lvert S\right\rvert_{G}:=\sum_{u\in S}d_{u}$ . The isoperimetric dimension of $G$ is given by

$$ \operatorname{Dim}(G):=\sup\left\{d\geq 1:\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V\\
0<\left\lvert S\right\rvert<\infty\end{subarray}}\frac{\left\lvert\partial S\right\rvert}{\left\lvert S\right\rvert_{G}^{\frac{d-1}{d}}}>0\right\}. $$

- 1. We remark that the uniform critical parameter $p^{*}_{c}(G)$ slightly differs from the most classical (non-uniform) one given by $p_{c}(G):=\inf\{p\in[0,1]:\theta(p)>0\}$ , where $\theta(p):=\sup_{v\in V}\theta_{v}(p)$ . However, these notions often coincide, such as for (quasi-)transitive graphs. See the introduction of [DGRSY20] for a survey of the rich history of the “ $p_{c}<1$ ” question and its place in statistical mechanics. Let us just recall that all of the results about percolation here can be translated into analogous statements about many other models, most notably the Ising model.

- 2. Duminil-Copin, Goswami, Raoufi, Severo, and Yadin proved that every quasi-transitive graph of superlinear growth satisfies $p_{c}<1$ [DGRSY20]. This had previously been a long-standing conjecture of Benjamini and Schramm [BS96]. In fact, the authors of [DGRSY20] established that $p^{*}_{c}<1$ for every (not necessarily transitive) bounded degree graph $G$ satisfying $\operatorname{Dim}(G)>4$ , and this was known to imply the conjecture about transitive graphs by the classical works of Gromov [Gro81] and Trofimov [Tro84].

## 3. Background and notation

In this section, we fix $G=(V,E)$ a locally finite, connected graph.

### Paths and connectivity

Let $S\subset V$ , $u,v\in S$ . A path from $u$ to $v$ in $S$ is a finite sequence $\gamma=(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\ell})$ of distinct vertices of $S$ such that $\gamma_{0}=u$ , $\gamma_{\ell}=v$ and $\{\gamma_{i-1},\gamma_{i}\}\in E$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}$ . When such a path exists, we say that $u$ is connected to $v$ in $S$ . By extension, a set $A$ is said to be connected to a set $B$ in $S$ if there exists a vertex of $A$ that is connected to a vertex of $B$ in $S$ . A path from $u$ to $\infty$ in $S$ is an infinite sequence of distinct vertices $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\ldots$ in $S$ such that $\gamma_{0}=u$ and $\{\gamma_{i-1},\gamma_{i}\}\in E$ for every $i\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$ . When such a path exists, we say that $u$ is connected to $\infty$ in $S$ .

### Exposed boundary

Let $S\subset V$ be a finite set. The exposed boundary of $S$ is the set $\partial_{\infty}S$ of all the edges $\{u,v\}$ such that $u\in S$ and $v$ is connected to $\infty$ in $V\setminus S$ . Notice that the exposed boundary is a subset of the standard boundary defined at the beginning of Section 2: for every finite set $S\subset V$ , we have $\partial_{\infty}S\subset\partial S$ .

### Percolation configurations

An element $\omega\in\{0,1\}^{E}$ is called a percolation configuration. Given such a configuration, an edge $e\in E$ is said to be open if $\omega(e)=1$ and closed if $\omega(e)=0$ . By extension, a path is said to be open if all its edges are open. The cluster of a vertex $u\in V$ is the connected component of $u$ in the graph $(V,\{e\in E\>:\>\omega(e)=1\})$ .

### Percolation events

A measurable subset $A\subset\{0,1\}^{E}$ is called a percolation event. Given $S\subset V$ and $u,v\in S$ , we denote by $u\xleftrightarrow{S}v$ the event that there exists an open path from $u$ to $v$ in $S$ , and simply write $u\xleftrightarrow{}v$ when $S=V$ . Finally, $u\xleftrightarrow{}\infty$ denotes the event that there exists an open path from $u$ to $\infty$ in $V$ .

### Percolation measures

A percolation measure on $G$ is a probability measure on the product space $\{0,1\}^{E}$ . For $p\in[0,1]$ , we denote by $\mathrm{P}_{p}$ the standard Bernoulli percolation measure, under which each edge is open with probability $p$ independently of the other edges.

### Positive association

A percolation event $\mathcal{E}$ is called increasing if for all percolation configurations $\omega,\xi$ satisfying $\omega\leq\xi$ for the standard product (partial) ordering, we have $\omega\in\mathcal{E}\implies\xi\in\mathcal{E}$ . Typical examples of increasing events are the connection events (such as $u\xleftrightarrow{S}v$ ) introduced above. A percolation measure $\mathrm{P}$ is said to be positively associated if

$$ \mathrm{P}[\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{F}]\geq\mathrm{P}[\mathcal{E}]\mathrm{P}[\mathcal{F}] $$

for all increasing events $\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F}$ . This property is often referred to as the FKG inequality. We will use that Bernoulli percolation $\mathrm{P}_{p}$ is positively associated (for every fixed $p\in[0,1]$ ) as established by Harris [Har60].

## 4. Exposed boundaries and cutsets

In this section, we fix $G=(V,E)$ an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. In our paper, we will use that minimal cutsets can be obtained by considering the exposed boundary of finite connected sets. In this section, we recall some well-known facts relating the two notions. The first elementary result is that the exposed boundary of a finite connected set is a minimal cutset.

#### Lemma 1.

Let $S\subset V$ be a finite connected set. For every $u\in S$ , $\partial_{\infty}S$ is a minimal cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ .

#### Proof.

Any path from $u$ to $\infty$ in $V$ must traverse an edge in $\partial_{\infty}S$ (consider the last edge traversed by this path intersecting $S$ ). Therefore, $\partial_{\infty}S$ is a cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ . To prove that it is minimal, consider an edge $e\in\partial_{\infty}S$ . Since $S$ is connected, there exists a path from $u$ to an endpoint of $e$ in $S$ and by definition of the exposed boundary, there must exist a path from the other endpoint of $e$ to $\infty$ in $V\setminus S$ . The concatenation of these two paths with $e$ connects $u$ to $\infty$ without using any edges of $\partial_{\infty}S$ other than $e$ . Hence $\partial_{\infty}S\setminus\{e\}$ is not a cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ . ∎

The second elementary result identifies the exposed boundary under some simple conditions.

#### Lemma 2.

Let $u\in V$ , let $\Pi$ be a minimal cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ . Let $A$ be the connected component of $u$ in $(V,E\setminus\Pi)$ and $B=\{e\cap A,\,e\in\Pi\}$ be the set of inner vertices of $\Pi$ . For every set $S$ of vertices, we have

$$ (B\subset S\subset A)\implies(\partial_{\infty}S=\Pi). $$

#### Proof.

Since $A$ is a maximal connected set in $(V,E\setminus\Pi)$ , all the edges at the boundary of $A$ belong to $\Pi$ , and therefore $\partial_{\infty}A\subset\partial A\subset\Pi$ . By Lemma 1, $\partial_{\infty}A$ is a cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ , hence, by the minimality of $\Pi$ , the two inclusions above must be equalities:

$$ \partial_{\infty}A=\partial A=\Pi. $$

Now, let $S$ be a set satisfying $B\subset S\subset A$ . Let $e\in\Pi$ . Since $e\in\partial_{\infty}A$ , one endpoint of $e$ must belong to $B$ and the other endpoint is connected to $\infty$ in $V\setminus A$ . Therefore, by hypothesis, one endpoint of $e$ belongs to $S$ and the other endpoint is connected to $\infty$ in $V\setminus S$ . This proves the inclusion

$$ \Pi\subset\partial_{\infty}S. $$

Let $e\in\partial_{\infty}S$ . Let $u$ be the endpoint of $e$ in $S$ , and let $v$ be the endpoint of $e$ connected to $\infty$ in $V\backslash S$ . Then, by hypothesis, $u\in A$ and $v$ is connected to $\infty$ in $V\backslash B$ . Since $\Pi=\partial A$ , every edge in $\Pi$ intersects $A$ and hence intersects $B$ . Therefore, there must exist an infinite path starting at $v$ in the subgraph $(V,E\backslash\Pi)$ . In particular, $v\not\in A$ , and hence $e\in\partial A=\Pi$ . This proves that the inclusion above must be an equality.

∎

## 5. Full connectivity via positive association

In this section, we consider the following problem: Let $B$ be a finite set in a graph, and $\mathrm{P}$ be a percolation measure. What is the probability that all the vertices of $B$ are all connected to each other? Or, in other words, what is the probability that all the vertices of $B$ lie in the same cluster? We prove that this probability is at least exponential in the size of $B$ when the measure is positively associated, and the probability for a point to be connected to $B$ is uniformly lower bounded. This result, formally stated below, will allow us to construct random sets with a prescribed boundary.

#### Proposition 3.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite, connected graph. Let $\mathrm{P}$ be a positively associated percolation measure on $G$ . Let $B\subset V$ , let $\theta,p\in(0,1]$ and suppose that $\mathrm{P}(u\leftrightarrow B)\geq\theta$ for every $u\in V$ , and $\mathrm{P}(e\text{ is open})\geq p$ for every $e\in E$ . Then for every $o\in V$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{o\leftrightarrow b\}\right)\geq c^{|B|}, $$

where $c:=\left(\frac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{3/\theta}$ .

#### Proof.

Say that a finite sequence of vertices $x_{1},\dots,x_{k}$ is chained if $x_{1}=o$ and for all $i\in\{2,\dots,k\}$ ,

$$ \frac{p\theta}{2}\leq\mathrm{P}\left(x_{i}\leftrightarrow\{x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1}\}\right)\leq\frac{\theta}{2}. $$

Since there exists at least one chained sequence (take $k=1$ ) and $V$ is finite, there must exist a chained sequence $x_{1},\dots,x_{k}$ that is maximal in the sense that for every vertex $x_{k+1}$ , the sequence $x_{1},\dots,x_{k+1}$ is not chained. Fix a maximal chained sequence $x_{1},\dots,x_{k}$ , and let $X:=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\}$ . We claim that, in addition to (P1), this sequence satisfies the following two properties, where $n:=\left\lvert B\right\rvert$ :

$$ \displaystyle\forall u\in V\quad\mathrm{P}(u\xleftrightarrow{}X)\geq\frac{\theta}{2}, \displaystyle k\leq\frac{2n}{\theta}. $$

To prove (P2), consider the set of vertices $W\subset V$ that are connected to $X$ with probability at least $\theta/2$ and suppose for contradiction that $W\neq V$ . Since $W$ is non empty (because $X\subset V$ ) and $G$ is connected, we can consider an edge $\{u,v\}$ such that $u\in W$ and $v\notin W$ . By positive association,

$$ \theta/2>\mathrm{P}(v\leftrightarrow X)\geq\mathrm{P}(\{u,v\}\text{ is open})\cdot\mathrm{P}(u\leftrightarrow X)\geq\frac{p\theta}{2}. $$

In particular, $x_{1},\dots,x_{k},v$ is a chained sequence, contradicting the maximality of $x_{1},\dots,x_{k}$ .

We now prove (P3). To this aim, for each $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ , let $N_{i}$ denote the number of clusters that intersect both $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{i}\}$ and $B$ . For every $i\in\{2,\dots,k\}$ , the increment $N_{i}-N_{i-1}$ is equal to $1$ if $x_{i}$ is connected to $B$ but not to the previous points $\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}\}$ , and it is equal to $0$ otherwise. Therefore, for every $i\in\{2,\ldots,k\}$ , we have the deterministic inequality

$$ N_{i}-N_{i-1}\geq\mathbf{1}_{x_{i}\xleftrightarrow{}B}-\mathbf{1}_{x_{i}\xleftrightarrow{}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}\}}. $$

Taking the expectation, using our hypothesis and (P1), for every $i\in\{2,\ldots,k\}$ , we get

$$ \mathrm{E}(N_{i})-\mathrm{E}(N_{i-1})\geq\underbrace{\mathrm{P}(x_{i}\xleftrightarrow{}B)}_{\geq\theta}-\underbrace{\mathrm{P}(x_{i}\xleftrightarrow{}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}\})}_{\leq\theta/2}\geq\theta/2. $$

Summing over $i\in\{2,\ldots,k\}$ and using $\mathrm{E}(N_{1})=\mathrm{P}(x_{1}\xleftrightarrow{}B)\geq\theta\geq\theta/2$ , we get $\mathrm{E}[N_{k}]\geq\frac{\theta}{2}k$ . Since $N_{k}$ is deterministically bounded above by $|B|=n$ , this concludes the proof of (P3).

We now explain how the three properties above of the chained sequence imply the desired lower bound in the proposition. First, we estimate the event that all the vertices of $X$ are connected to $o$ : By (P1), (P3) and positive association, we have

$$ \mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{u\in X}\{o\xleftrightarrow{}u\}\right)\geq\prod_{i=2}^{k}\mathrm{P}\left(x_{i}\leftrightarrow\{x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1}\}\right)\geq\left(\frac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{k-1}\geq\left(\frac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{\frac{2n}{\theta}}. $$

Second, we estimate the event that all the vertices of $B$ are connected to $X$ : By (P2) and positive association, we have

$$ \mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{b\leftrightarrow X\}\right)\geq\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{n}. $$

If all the vertices of $X$ are connected to $o$ and all the vertices of $B$ are connected to $X$ , then all the vertices of $B$ are connected to $o$ . Hence, by the two displayed equations above and positive association, we obtain

$$ \mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{o\leftrightarrow b\}\right)\geq\mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{u\in X}\{o\xleftrightarrow{}u\}\right)\cdot\mathrm{P}\left(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{b\leftrightarrow X\}\right)\geq\left(\frac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{\frac{2n}{\theta}}\cdot\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{n}\geq c^{n}, $$

where $c:=\left(\frac{p\theta}{2}\right)^{3/\theta}$ . ∎

## 6. Proof of Theorem 1

Let $G=(V,E)$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. In this section, we prove Theorem 1, in the following form.

$$ \big(\exists p<1\ \exists\theta>0\ \forall u\in V\quad\mathrm{P}_{p}(u\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq\theta\big)\iff\big(\exists K<\infty\ \forall u\in V\ \forall n\geq 1\quad|\mathcal{Q}_{n}(u)|\leq K^{n}\big). $$

The implication $\Leftarrow$ is well-known, and follows from the Peierls argument [Ben13, Theorem 4.11], which we now recall for completeness. Let $u\in V$ . If the cluster of $u$ is finite, then by Lemma 1, its exposed boundary is a finite minimal cutset from $u$ to $\infty$ , and all its edges are closed. Hence, by the union bound, for every $p\in[0,1]$ we have

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(|C_{u}|<\infty)\leq\sum_{n\geq 1}q_{n}(1-p)^{n}. $$

If $q_{n}\leq K^{n}$ for some constant $K<\infty$ , then the right hand side above converges to $0$ as $p$ tends to $1$ . Since the bound is uniform in $u$ , there exists $p<1$ such that

$$ \forall u\in V\quad\mathrm{P}_{p}(u\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq 1/2. $$

We now prove the implication $\Rightarrow$ . Fix $\theta,p\in(0,1)$ such that $\mathrm{P}_{p}(u\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq\theta$ for every $u\in V$ . Fix $o\in V$ and $n\geq 1$ . Writing $C$ for the cluster of $o$ , we show that for every minimal cutset $\Pi$ from $o$ to $\infty$ with $\left\lvert\Pi\right\rvert=n$ ,

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\partial_{\infty}C=\Pi)\geq 1/K^{n}, $$

where $K=K(p,\theta)\in(0,\infty)$ is a finite constant depending on $p$ and $\theta$ only (in particular it does not depend on the chosen vertex $o$ ). This concludes the proof since

$$ 1\geq\sum_{\Pi\in\mathcal{Q}_{n}(o)}\mathrm{P}_{p}(\partial_{\infty}C=\Pi)\overset{\penalty\ \eqref{eq:8}}{\geq}|\mathcal{Q}_{n}(o)|/K^{n}. $$

Let us now prove the lower bound (17). As in Lemma 2, let $A$ be the connected component of $o$ in $(V,E\setminus\Pi)$ and $B$ the set of inner vertices of $\Pi$ . Since any infinite open path from a vertex $u\in A$ must intersect $B$ before exiting $A$ , the hypothesis $\mathrm{P}_{p}(u\leftrightarrow\infty)\geq\theta$ implies

$$ \forall u\in A\quad\mathrm{P}_{p}(u\xleftrightarrow{A}B)\geq\theta. $$

Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the event that every vertex in $B$ is connected to $o$ by an open path in $A$ . By Proposition 3 applied to the finite subgraph of $G$ induced by $A$ , we have $\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{E})\geq c^{n}$ , where $c=(p\theta/2)^{3/\theta}>0$ . Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the event that all the edges of $\Pi$ are closed. By independence, we have

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{F})=\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{E})\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{F})\geq c^{n}(1-p)^{n}. $$

If the event $\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{F}$ occurs, then the cluster $C$ of $o$ satisfies $B\subset C\subset A$ . Hence, by Lemma 2 we must have $\partial_{\infty}C=\Pi$ . This concludes that

$$ \mathrm{P}_{p}(\partial_{\infty}C=\Pi)\geq\mathrm{P}_{p}(\mathcal{E}\cap\mathcal{F})\geq c^{n}(1-p)^{n}, $$

which establishes the desired lower bound (17) with $K=\frac{1}{c(1-p)}=\frac{1}{(p\theta/2)^{3/\theta}(1-p)}$ .
